Article Title: Inspiring story of the day: “Having a dad with a big name doesn’t do the work for you” - How Trinity Rodman rose above Dennis Rodman’s shadow, lived in motels, and built her own soccer legacy
Article Text:
Inspiring story of the day: “Having a dad with a big name doesn’t do the work for you” - How Trinity Rodman rose above Dennis Rodman’s shadow, lived in motels, and built her own soccer legacy

How did Trinity Rodman live in a car despite being Dennis Rodman’s daughter

Call Her Daddy

What did Trinity Rodman say about her relationship with Dennis Rodman

Why does Trinity Rodman call Michelle Moyer her role model?

How did Trinity Rodman turn a difficult childhood into a soccer career

Why is Trinity Rodman’s story inspiring beyond soccer

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Trinity Rodman has built a soccer career that now stands on its own. The Washington Spirit star is a 2024 Olympic gold medalist, a 2021 NWSL champion and, as of January 2026, the highest-paid player in NWSL history. But her childhood looked very different from what many people expected from the daughter of NBA legend Dennis Rodman . Trinity and her brother DJ once lived with their mother, Michelle Moyer, in a Ford Expedition and cheap motels in Newport Beach. Through those difficult years, Michelle kept life feeling normal for her children. That bond helped shape Trinity into the player she is today.Having a famous father did not mean Trinity Rodman grew up with an easy life. After Dennis Rodman and Michelle Moyer separated, Trinity, her brother DJ and their mother faced serious money problems. For a period, they moved between a Ford Expedition and motels when Michelle could afford a room.The situation was especially strange because they were living in Newport Beach, where Trinity went to a wealthy school. She has spoken about seeing classmates arrive in expensive cars while her own family was trying to work out where they would stay.On, Trinity explained just how unusual those years were:“We had a Ford Expedition and we lived in that for a little bit. Mind you, in Newport Beach… So imagine living in a car going to a rich school when everybody else is in Rolls-Royces and Range Rovers. But my mom tried to make every situation seem smoother than it actually was. For me and DJ, it was never embarrassing because we had each other and we had our mom.”For Trinity and DJ, however, those memories were not only painful. Their mother tried hard to make sure they still had happy childhood moments. At motels, they could eat breakfast, use the pool and spend time together before school. That helped the children see their family life differently from how an outsider might have seen it.Trinity’s relationship with Dennis Rodman has remained one of the most talked-about parts of her story, but it has also been one of the most painful. She has said that her father was often absent while she was growing up and that there were long periods when they had little contact.That distance became impossible to ignore as Trinity began making a name for herself in soccer. Instead of being known only as an athlete, she was repeatedly asked about being Dennis Rodman’s daughter.She later spoke openly about how difficult that connection could feel:“He’s a person. He’s not a dad. Maybe by blood, but nothing else… Hearing his voice is painful because it’s missing him mixed with the fact that he’s an alcoholic. I answer the phone now for my conscience, but it took me a long time to realize that having a dad with a big name doesn’t do the work for you. I had to build everything myself.”Dennis has also publicly admitted that he was not the father he wanted to be. At his Basketball Hall of Fame induction, he said he wished he had been a better father.For Trinity, though, her own career could not depend on her father’s reputation. Her speed, finishing, attacking ability and work on the field became the things that made people remember her.If Dennis Rodman gave Trinity a famous last name, Michelle Moyer gave her the support that helped her grow into a professional athlete. Michelle raised Trinity and DJ largely as a single mother and remained closely involved in Trinity’s soccer journey.The Guardian reported in 2021 that Trinity saw her mother as her main support system. That feeling has remained central to how she talks about her childhood and her success.Trinity put it simply:“My mom wasn’t in the NBA, but she’s my role model. She is my world, my rock, and my right hand. She’s the strongest person I know. People always say, ‘Oh, you get your athleticism from your dad,’ but my work ethic, my heart, my grit, and the woman I am today-that’s 100% my mom.”That is an important part of Trinity Rodman’s story because her biggest influence was not another famous athlete. It was the person who was there when money was tight, when the family had nowhere stable to stay and when Trinity was still only a young girl trying to understand her world.Trinity’s soccer career moved quickly once she reached the professional level. She entered the NWSL with the Washington Spirit in 2021 and became the youngest player ever selected in the league’s draft at the time. She went on to win the NWSL Rookie of the Year award and helped the Spirit win the league championship that same year.Her rise continued with the U.S. women’s national team. She became an important attacking player for the USWNT and was part of the squad that won Olympic gold at the 2024 Paris Games.The success also changed the way her name was viewed. Instead of being introduced mainly as Dennis Rodman’s daughter, Trinity became a major soccer star in her own right.In January 2026, she reached another major point in her career when she re-signed with the Washington Spirit on a deal worth more than $2 million per year. The agreement made her the highest-paid player in NWSL history.That achievement says a lot about how far she has come. The girl who once went to school after sleeping in a car is now one of the biggest names in American women’s soccer.Trinity Rodman’s story is not simply about becoming famous despite having a difficult childhood. It is about how she chose to define herself.She could have spent her career being introduced through her father’s name. Instead, she has built an identity around her own performances and the people who stood beside her. Her mother remained a constant presence, while soccer gave Trinity a place where her effort could speak for itself.Her journey also explains why the success means more than trophies and contracts. The Olympic gold medal, NWSL championship and record-breaking deal are major achievements, but they came after years of work that had little to do with her father’s fame.Trinity has been clear about that point herself: a famous parent can give someone a name, but it cannot do the training, handle the pressure or play the game for them.For Trinity Rodman, the most important part of her legacy may be that she did not allow her father’s story to become her own. She took the difficult parts of her childhood, held on to the support her mother gave her and built a career that now belongs completely to her.
Article Summary: Trinity rodman has built a soccer career that now stands on its own. The washington spirit star is a 2024 olympic gold medalist, a 2021 nwsl champion and the highest-paid player in nwsl history. But her childhood looked very different from what many people expected from the daughter of nba legend dennis rodman.

Article Title: Who is Joanna Wietrzyk? Australian HYROX athlete and fitness coach at centre of Beijing controversy
Article Text:
Who is Joanna Wietrzyk? Australian HYROX athlete and fitness coach at centre of Beijing controversy

Who is Joanna Wietrzyk? Australian HYROX athlete and fitness coach

What happened to Joanna Wietrzyk at HYROX Beijing?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has become the focus of attention after a controversial finish at the HYROX Beijing fitness race on September 12, 2026. Wietrzyk, who competed in the Women’s Pro division, reportedly suffered bowel incontinence during the race but continued through the course and finished in 1:01:23. The incident drew strong reactions because HYROX uses shared running lanes and workout equipment, including rowing machines, sleds and mats. HYROX China said the affected area was isolated and disinfected, while equipment was removed and replaced. The organizer did not publicly name the athlete in its statement.Joanna Wietrzyk is an Australian elite fitness racing athlete, strength and conditioning coach and competitor in the international HYROX and functional fitness scene. She has a background in CrossFit, functional bodybuilding and competitive athletics before moving into hybrid endurance racing.Wietrzyk competes in the Women’s Pro division, the higher-level category of HYROX competition. Her races combine running with workout stations, and she has built a reputation for strong performances across the sled and ergometer sections. In 2026, she competed at major events including Phoenix, Warsaw and the World Championships.She won the Warsaw Major and set the Women’s Solo Pro world record with 54:25.Away from competition, Wietrzyk works as an online performance coach and personal trainer. Her work includes race preparation, hybrid endurance and strength training.The controversy began after photos and videos from the September 12 HYROX Beijing event spread on social media. They appeared to show Wietrzyk continuing to race after suffering bowel incontinence. She carried on with movements including burpees, and reports said the incident affected parts of the course and equipment used by athletes behind her.That led to two different reactions. Some people praised Wietrzyk for finishing despite an extremely difficult moment. Others questioned why the race continued while shared areas and equipment could have been affected. The debate also raised questions about how HYROX should handle a hygiene or safety problem during a live race.HYROX China responded on September 12, saying the affected area and lanes were sealed off and isolated as soon as possible. The organizer said it carried out full disinfection through the end of the day’s events and removed and replaced the relevant equipment. It also said the entire carpet would be replaced after the competition, followed by deep cleaning and disinfection.Reports identifying the athlete as Wietrzyk also said she won the Women’s Pro race in 1:01:23. HYROX’s official event page confirms that the Women’s Pro race took place on September 12, but its public event information does not identify Wietrzyk in connection with the incident.After the race, Wietrzyk reportedly shared a hospital-bed selfie with the message, “A win is a win.” The post added another layer to the online debate, with some readers seeing it as determination and others questioning the decision to continue racing.
Article Summary: Joanna wietrzyk is an australian elite fitness racing athlete, strength and conditioning coach and competitor in the international hyrox and functional fitness scene. She has a background in crossfit, functional bodybuilding and competitive athletics before moving into hybrid endurance racing.

Article Title: “It’s huge for me, it means standing alongside women”: How Angel Reese is building a global sports empire through major ownership moves beyond the WNBA
Article Text:
How Angel Reese is building a global sports empire through major ownership moves beyond the WNBA(Getty Images)

From DC Power FC to TOGETHXR , Angel Reese keeps building beyond basketball

Angel Reese is building a name for herself far beyond the basketball court. The WNBA star has already stepped into sports ownership in the US, and her latest move has taken that business journey overseas.In March 2026, Reese joined the ownership group of the Brisbane Bullets in Australia. The move added professional basketball in another country to a growing portfolio that includes soccer and women’s sports media.The Brisbane Bullets announced on March 10, 2026, that Angel Reese had joined the club’s ownership group. She joined majority owner Jason Levien and co-owner Ben Haan, with the group also pursuing a new WNBL team in Brisbane.That makes the deal more than a simple investment for Reese. The Brisbane Bullets compete in Australia’s National Basketball League, while the ownership group has also been working toward bringing a women’s team to the city through a bid for the WNBL’s 10th license.The move also followed Reese’s visit to Australia with Reebok. She promoted new colorways of her Angel Reese 1 signature shoe during the trip. Reebok also announced a footwear partnership with the WNBL that will begin in 2027.Brisbane Bullets CEO Malcolm Watts welcomed Reese to the group and highlighted what her profile could bring to basketball in Queensland.“Angel is a fantastic ambassador for basketball and a globally recognised superstar,” Watts said in the Bullets’ announcement. He also pointed to basketball’s growth in Queensland and the message Reese can send to young players in Brisbane.The Bullets also announced Will Weaver as their president of basketball operations and head coach on March 10, giving the organization another major change around the same time Reese joined its ownership group.The Brisbane investment follows two earlier ownership moves. Angel Reese joined the ownership group of DC Power FC in 2024, giving her a stake in professional soccer while she continued her WNBA career.Then, in September 2025, she joined the ownership group of TOGETHXR, the sports media and lifestyle company founded by Sue Bird, Alex Morgan, Simone Manuel and Chloe Kim.Angel Reese explained what the opportunity meant to her while explaining what it meant for her:“It’s huge for me,” Angel Reese said. “It means standing alongside women who aren’t just legends in their sports, but real trailblazers in business and culture. They’ve opened doors for so many of us, and now I get to lock arms with them and keep pushing things forward.”She also explained that she wanted to bring her own perspective to the established group rather than simply step into someone else’s role.“It’s not so much about teaching them as it is about joining them, and bringing a fresh perspective into everything they’ve already been doing so well,” Reese told USA TODAY Sports in the same interview.Her business work also connects with her foundation. Reese founded the Angel C. Reese Foundation in 2023, with a focus on empowering girls and women through sports, education and financial literacy.Now, the Brisbane Bullets give Angel Reese another link to the sports business world, this time outside the United States. Now she remains a key player for Atlanta Dream but her growing ownership portfolio shows that she is already building opportunities beyond her WNBA career.At 24, Angel Reese has moved into soccer, sports media and international basketball while continuing to develop her own brand. The Brisbane deal adds another major piece to that picture.

The wnba star has already stepped into sports ownership in the us, and her latest move has taken that business journey overseas. Reese joined the ownership group of dc power fc in 2024, giving her a stake in professional soccer while she continued her wnba career.

Article Title: 'We meet everyone': Mohsin Naqvi meets BCCI's Rajeev Shukla, Devajit Saikia after Asia Cup final as Indian team skip trophy ceremony
Article Text:
Mohsin Naqvi, Devajit Saikia. (Photo/screengrab)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Asia Cup trophy drama continued for the second year in a row after Indian women's cricket team did not receive the trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi following their title win in Dubai on Sunday.Harmanpreet Kaur-led India beat Sri Lanka by 72 runs to win a record-extending eighth Women's Asia Cup title. But after the match, the Indian players did not return to the field for the presentation ceremony where Naqvi, who is also the Pakistan Cricket Board chairman and Pakistan's interior minister, was present.Hours after the final, BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia defended the decision, saying situation has changed after the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack.“Our men’s team won the Asia Cup a year and a half ago. And our whole situation, since the April 2025 Pahalgam incident, changed after that. So, after that, there was pressure on us from our citizens that we shouldn’t keep any relations with our neighboring country and not play cricket with them. But our government has a policy that we must play against every country in multinational tournaments,” Saikia told news agency IANS.“But that doesn’t mean we will follow every condition laid out for us. Our military conflict is still ongoing. One of the main leaders who is working against the interests of our country; we can’t receive the trophy from him. The Women’s team has expressed solidarity with the decision taken by the men’s team last year,” Saikia said.However, television cameras showed Saikia meeting Naqvi during the match. As players shook hands after the final, the broadcast showed the Royal Box at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium, where Naqvi first greeted BCCI vice-president Rajeev Shukla and then had a conversation with Saikia.Asked about that meeting, Saikia said it was part of normal match-day protocol and did not contradict the BCCI's stand on the trophy presentation."It's not as if we wouldn't meet anyone. I was sitting outside in the Royal Box seats right from the toss until the end of the game. Having sat there, I remained in that same place throughout the match. Everyone who came met me during the match; someone sat next to me, then Rajeev Shukla came and sat with me. The person you mentioned (Naqvi) also came and sat alongside deputy chairman Khalid Sahib. That's just a normal tradition—whenever anyone comes, we meet and talk with everyone. "It may be recalled that the Indian men’s team had last year declined to receive the Asia Cup trophy and medals from Naqvi, who heads the Pakistan Cricket Board and is also the Interior Minister of that country.The Indian team is yet to receive the Asia Cup trophy, which has since been kept in the ACC office.Instead the Suryakumar Yadav-led Indian side conducted an impromptu celebration on the dais without the physical prize.However, this time the Indian women’s team members did not even return to the ground after BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia presented Nandini Sharma with an in-house best fielder medal.
Article Summary: Indian women's cricket team did not receive the trophy from mohsin naqvi following their title win in dubai on sunday.naqvi is also the pakistan cricket board chairman and pakistan's interior minister. Bcci secretary devajit saikia defended the decision, saying situation has changed after the 2025 pahalgam terror attack.

India's next Test assignment will take them to New Zealand for a two-match series beginning November 19, and former Kiwi fast bowler Trent Boult believes KL Rahul will be one of the Indian batters worth watching closely.The two Tests will form part of India's marathon New Zealand tour, which begins on October 22 and features 12 matches across the three formats. With India needing a strong result to remain in contention for the World Test Championship (WTC) final, the spotlight is expected to fall on several key players, including captain Shubman Gill and pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah .Boult, however, has picked Rahul and his opening partner Yashasvi Jaiswal as the two Indian batters he is particularly looking forward to seeing in action."I'm always a big fan of KL Rahul and his style of batsmanship. So he's a big player at the top of the order for the Indian side. And yeah, I believe Jaiswal is there as well. Two classy batters to see bat. So yeah, be interesting to see," Boult said in an interview to PTI.The timing of the series could make conditions particularly interesting. Unlike India's previous Test tours of New Zealand, which have often taken place in the February-March window, this series will be played in late October and November.Boult feels the timing could bring colder weather into play, while he is hoping the New Zealand pitches retain some grass and offer assistance to the home attack."It's always an exciting chance when the Indian team comes down to play Test cricket in New Zealand," Boult said."The only thing I can see happening is it's going to be late October. I believe, just coming out of winter. So it's going to be quite cold. Hopefully, there's a bit of greenness in the wickets for some of our bowlers. It's going to be a good series, I'm sure," the star former Kiwi pacer added.Boult also backed the current New Zealand bowling unit to make an impact against India, pointing to the variety available to the team.Kyle Jamieson, Matt Henry, Nathan Smith and Will O'Rourke bring different qualities to the attack, and Boult believes that gives New Zealand enough options to develop its own identity."I think the bowling is very well balanced. It's got bases covered in terms of a good pace, obviously, with Will O'Rourke. Obviously, a bit of swing and a bit of bounce from Kyle Jamieson and Matt Henry with his accuracy."So yeah, I think the way me, Tim (Southee) and Wags (Neil Wagner) did it over the years was a unique way in itself. But there's other strengths and other game plans that our younger bowlers can follow," Boult further said.

Former kiwi fast bowler trent boult believes kl rahul will be one of the indian batters worth watching closely. Kolkata: Almost fourteen years after Ishank Jaggi was named Player of the Match when East Zone last won the Duleep Trophy, he watched Ishan Kishan collect the same award as the region ended its long wait for the title.For Jaggi, the coincidence was nostalgic. But more than the memories of his own playing days, seeing someone he considers a younger brother reach the summit gave him more satisfaction.With their similar names — Ishank and Ishan — adding a little coincidence to a bond that has grown from being teammates to mentor and student, Jaggi has known Kishan since the latter was around 16. He was one of the young wicketkeeper-batter’s first senior teammates and, over the years, their relationship evolved from dressing-room association to a much closer bond. Jaggi later worked with Kishan at his cricket academy and also played a role in his development as a coach.That has given Jaggi a ringside view of Kishan’s journey — from an exciting, aggressive young batter to a more mature all-format cricketer.“Ishan always had that fighting spirit and hunger. That was never missing. What has changed is the experience and maturity he has gained,” Jaggi said.Kishan’s difficult phase after losing his place in the India side and his BCCI central contract in 2024, according to Jaggi, became an important turning point.“Sometimes when you hit rock bottom, you start thinking more deeply about your game and your career,” he said. Rather than allowing the setback to derail him, Kishan used the period to work on several aspects of his game. Jaggi said the batter put considerable effort into his batting, fitness, nutrition and preparation, while also developing a better understanding of his own game.The biggest change, Jaggi believes, has been in Kishan’s ability to temper his natural aggression according to the demands of a situation. “He was always seen as an attacking player, but over the last couple of years he has shown that he can also build an innings and play according to what the team requires,” Jaggi said.His stint with Sunrisers Hyderabad also helped in that evolution. At Mumbai Indians, Kishan had been part of a star-studded batting line-up. With SRH, he was entrusted with greater responsibility as stand-in skipper in Pat Cummins’ absence in the early part of 2026 IPL, something Jaggi feels accelerated his growth.“Responsibility often helps a player grow,” he said.The results have been visible since Kishan began his comeback through domestic grind and then grabbed the opportunities that came his way. His performances eventually took him back into India’s plans, culminating in his return to the national T20 setup.For Jaggi, however, the journey is personal as much as professional.When East Zone reached this year’s Duleep Trophy final, someone tagged Jaggi on social media, reminding him of his own Player of the Match performance in the 2012 final. It was only then that he realised how striking the parallel was.“I hadn’t really thought about it until someone tagged me,” Jaggi said.Jaggi had won the honour when they last lifted the trophy in Oct 2012. Almost fourteen years later, Kishan — the player he has known since his teenage years and later worked with as a coach — produced a match-winning performance in the final and claimed the same individual award.Yet, Jaggi insists he is not living in the past. “I’m more excited about the current team. My playing days are over, so there’s no point living in the past,” he said.Instead, his pride is centred on Kishan and the new generation he has seen emerge from Jharkhand.“More than anything, I’m happy for Ishan. He’s like a younger brother to me.”As Kishan lifted the trophy after leading East Zone to their first Duleep title in 14 editions, Jaggi could look back at the journey from a young player in the dressing room to a cricketer he helped nurture away from the spotlight.“It gives me immense satisfaction,” Jaggi said.For a coach-cum-mentor who had watched the highs and lows from close quarters, seeing Kishan turn adversity into a statement of maturity — and then repeat his own Duleep Trophy Player of the Match feat — made the moment all the more special.
Article Summary: Ishank jaggi was named player of the match when east zone last won the duleep trophy in oct 2012. He watched ishan kishan collect the same award as the region ended its long wait for the title. The coincidence was nostalgic. But more than the memories of his own playing days, seeing someone he considers a younger brother reach the summit gave him more satisfaction.

Article Title: In 1986, someone bought Super Mario Bros. as a Christmas gift and left it sealed in a desk drawer; 35 years later, the forgotten game sold for $660,000
Article Text:
Heritage Auctions said the copy was a pristine example of a particular Super Mario Bros. variant that was produced for an extraordinarily short period.

A short production run made it rare

A copy of Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. bought as a Christmas gift in late 1986 was placed inside a desk drawer and forgotten for 35 years. It remained sealed and untouched until it was discovered in 2021. On April 2 that year, the game sold for $660,000 at Heritage Auctions, setting a new record for the most ever paid for a video game.The game was sold as part of Heritage Auctions' Comics & Comic Art Auction in Dallas, Texas. The auction house described it as the finest known copy of the oldest sealed hangtab version of Super Mario Bros. to have been professionally graded for auction. The copy carried a Wata 9.6 A+ grade and was still sealed in its original packaging.The sale broke the previous record of $114,000, which had been set by another copy of Super Mario Bros. at a Heritage Auctions sale in July 2020. The 2021 copy was especially valuable because of its rare packaging variation and its condition.Someone bought the game in late 1986 as a Christmas gift. Instead of being opened, it was put into the bottom of an office desk drawer. It stayed there for decades without the owner realising that the unopened game could one day become a highly valuable collector's item.“It stayed in the bottom of my office desk this whole time since the day I bought it,” said the seller, who asked not to be identified. “I never thought anything about it,” he said as quoted by Heritage Auctions.The game's condition was only part of what made it special. Heritage Auctions said the copy was a pristine example of a particular Super Mario Bros. variant that was produced for an extraordinarily short period.It had a perforated cardboard hangtab and plastic shrink wrap. Heritage described it as the finest sealed copy with a perforated cardboard hangtab of any black box title it had offered. It was also the oldest factory-sealed copy of Super Mario Bros. ever offered by the auction house.The copy was produced in late 1986. According to Heritage Auctions Video Games Director Valarie McLeckie, it was among the earliest copies that came with plastic shrink wrap instead of a sticker seal.“This particular copy was produced in late 1986, and it was one of the earliest copies produced that had plastic shrink wrap, rather than sticker seal,” McLeckie said. “By early 1987, Nintendo was producing a version that had another new variation to their original packaging (an additional "code")."As soon as this copy of Super Mario Bros. arrived at Heritage, we knew the market would find it just as sensational as we did," Heritage Auctions Video Games Director Valarie McLeckie said. "Even so, the degree to which this game was embraced outside the market has been nothing short of exceptional, and that aspect of this sale has certainly exceeded our expectations. Though, I suppose we can't be too shocked; who doesn't love Mario?"
Article Summary: A copy of nintendo's super mario bros. bought as a christmas gift in late 1986 was placed inside a desk drawer and forgotten for 35 years. It remained sealed and untouched until it was discovered in 2021. On april 2 that year, the game sold for $660,000 at heritage auctions, setting a new record for the most ever paid for a video game.

Article Title: As Nike stock sees worst fall in its history, tech VC Chamath Palihapitiya on what went wrong with the American shoe giant: Somewhere along the way ...
Article Text:
Nike’s historic slide

Chamath Palihapitiya on Nike’s north star

Nike recently witnessed the worst fall in its stock history, raising questions about what went wrong for the American giant once synonymous with athletic excellence. The decline prompted sharp commentary from tech venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, who reflected on how the company lost sight of its original version. Palihapitiya argued that Nike’s early success was built on a clear North Star: “Somewhere along the way, mastery and excellence became too traditional looking. So they went to things that were just nothing to be associated with mastery or excellence. I don't aspire to be a fat person. Never have, never will. I aspire to be Michael Jordan. Always have, always will." He recalled growing up seeing icons like Michael Jordan, Tiger Woods, Serena Williams, and Pete Sampras, all representing the pinnacle of athletic achievement. “I don’t aspire to be a fat person. I aspire to be Michael Jordan,” he said, underscoring Nike’s original appeal as a brand tied to greatness.Nike shares have fallen roughly 78% from their November 2021 peak, a slide that market strategist Charlie Bilello has called the largest drawdown in the company's history as a publicly traded business — a notable distinction given that Nike has previously weathered recessions, boycotts, and supply chain disruptions without this level of sustained decline.The stock recently touched its lowest level in 12 years, erasing more than $200 billion in market value along the way.The pressure has shown up inside the company as well. According to Bloomberg reporting, CEO Elliott Hill told staff in an internal meeting earlier this year that he was worn out from constantly discussing how to fix the business, while stressing that employees couldn't simply assume everything was fine. Nike has been navigating a difficult stretch marked by shifting consumer preferences, intensifying competition from newer brands, supply chain adjustments, and a broader pivot toward direct-to-consumer sales — with sales in China falling for eight consecutive quarters and market share slipping to rivals like Hoka and On.Speaking about the decline, Palihapitiya argued that Nike's core problem traces back to losing sight of a clear guiding identity. He said that after nearly three decades in business, he's come to believe that having a clear North Star and sticking to it is essential — and that Nike's North Star, as he understood it growing up, was mastery and excellence expressed through athletics. He pointed to watching athletes like Michael Jordan, Tiger Woods, Serena Williams, and Pete Sampras as embodiments of that idea.At some point, Palihapitiya argued, that pursuit of mastery and excellence started to feel too conventional to the company, and Nike shifted toward messaging that had little connection to those qualities at all. He was blunt about his own take on that shift, saying plainly that his aspiration has always been to be like Michael Jordan, not to feel validated regardless of effort or achievement.He argued Nike should refocus on the idea that its role was never to make people feel good about themselves as they are, but to inspire people to improve by holding up genuinely elite athletes as the standard. Palihapitiya pointed to the sacrifice required of top athletes who dedicate their entire lives to mastering their craft, arguing Nike should embrace and take pride in that association rather than shy away from it — a positioning he believes has broad, universal appeal. He closed by reiterating that Nike's failure to stay anchored to that original identity of excellence and mastery is, in his view, at the heart of its current struggles.
Article Summary: Nike shares have fallen roughly 78% from their november 2021 peak. Tech venture capitalist chamath palihapitiya says the company lost sight of its original north star. He argued nike's north star, as he understood it growing up, was mastery and excellence.
